```
>>> val = np.random.rand(1000000)
>>> mask = val < 0.99
>>> val[mask] = np.nan
>>> arr = SparseArray(val)
>>> %timeit arr.argmax()
8.6 ms ± 343 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each) <- master
44.3 µs ± 934 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000 loops each) <- this pr
```

issue_context.title: ENH: implement efficient sorting methods for SparseArray (argsort/argmin/argmax)
issue_context.body:
xref https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/27801#discussion_r426017444

`SparseArray` currently does not implement `_values_for_argsort` or `argsort/`argmin`/`argmax` itself, which means it is using the base implementation, which converts the sparse array to a dense numpy array. Room for improvements thus.

review_comments: Can we also test an empty array input here?

As you mentioned below, `_first_fill_value_loc` appears to be named confusingly and does more work than needed (involves a sort as well). If you just want to see whether or not the fill value exists, could use `ngaps` or `npoints` on `self.sp_index` (for example as done in `_min_max` or `unique`)
No, actually the name is fine, but the doc and implementation is wrong. I do need to find the first position of the fill value in argmax/argmin instead of just checking the existence.

I can give you the example:
```
>>> arr = SparseArray([1, 2, 0, 0], fill_value=0)
>>> arr.argmin()
2
```
The candidate is 0 but fill_value is smaller, thus we return the result from _first_fill_value_loc().

Ok thanks for explaining, makes sense. Based on code in `SparseIndex`, for example https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/9f43ec6a98580d8f1c74d068afb31ec902c63e8c/pandas/_libs/sparse.pyx#L75, we should be guaranteed monotonically increasing indices. So is the first fill value location just `self.sp_index.indices[0]`?
`self.sp_index.indices[0]` is actually the first non-fill_value position, not the fill_value.
